pages.title: Restaurant prime cost: what to count and compare
pages.heading: Prime cost: check the inputs before the target.
pages.description: Calculate prime cost from comparable food, beverage, labor and sales records, then investigate the reason for a change.
pages.author: Ready Margin editorial
pages.takeaway: Use the same reporting period for cost of goods sold, labor and sales. Then investigate the change in each component.

sections.title: Calculate for one period
sections.body: Add cost of goods sold and total labor cost for the period. Divide by sales for those same dates and multiply by 100. The result combines major operating costs; it does not measure final profit.

sections.title: Define the included costs
sections.body: Agree the accounts and full employment-cost basis with the person preparing the report. Document inventory treatment, transfers, credits and incomplete invoices so comparisons use the same definitions.

sections.title: Check the cutoff
sections.body: Purchases, counts, payroll and sales must cover comparable dates. Mark estimates and resolve timing differences before interpreting a percentage change.

sections.title: Review food and labor separately
sections.body: Identify whether the movement came from sales, supplier costs, stock records, coverage or pay inputs. Use the source documents and operating context to select the next check.

sections.title: Set a restaurant-specific target
sections.body: Use your format, menu, service hours and staffing plan to establish a working target. Review the reason for departures rather than treating one benchmark as a diagnosis.

pages.title: Restaurant month-end close checklist
pages.heading: A month-end close checklist with responsibilities.
pages.description: Collect settlements, reconcile accounts and review bills and payroll before presenting the restaurant’s monthly reports.
pages.author: Ready Margin editorial
pages.takeaway: A close checklist needs source records, responsible people and an explicit list of what remains unresolved.

sections.title: Set the dates and contacts
sections.body: Name the reporting period, close date and person supplying each input. State which source is required and who can explain a difference.

sections.title: Reconcile sales and receipts
sections.body: Gather POS, settlement and delivery-platform statements with bank activity. Keep fees, refunds and timing differences attached to the relevant receipt.

sections.title: Review late costs
sections.body: Check supplier invoices, credits and payroll corrections. Agree the accounting treatment of costs belonging to the month when the final document has not arrived.

sections.title: Check accounts and locations
sections.body: Reconcile bank and card accounts, investigate unusual balances and confirm any inventory count dates. Apply consistent account and location mapping.

sections.title: Send the findings with the reports
sections.body: Include the agreed statements, material movements and outstanding questions. Label provisional figures and name the contact and next check for each open item.

pages.title: Restaurant recipe costing and portion review
pages.heading: Cost the recipe your kitchen actually serves.
pages.description: Use current ingredient prices, comparable units, usable yield and portion sizes for a repeatable recipe-cost calculation.
pages.author: Ready Margin editorial
pages.keyword: restaurant recipe costing and dish margin
pages.takeaway: Keep the purchase unit, usable yield and serving size consistent before comparing a dish’s ingredient cost with its selling price.

sections.title: Confirm the working recipe
sections.body: Check ingredients, preparation and portion size with the kitchen. Include batch components, sauces and garnishes. Date the recipe and record who confirmed it.

sections.title: Convert to comparable units
sections.body: Record the supplier pack size and convert case prices to the unit used in the recipe. Account for usable yield when trimming or preparation reduces the available quantity.

sections.title: Calculate the batch and portion
sections.body: Multiply usable ingredient unit cost by the amount used. Add those costs for the batch and divide by its usable portions. Keep the invoice and recipe beside the calculation.

sections.title: Read the margin in context
sections.body: Selling price less ingredients must still support labor and other operating costs. Compare the result with sales mix and the work required to prepare the dish.

sections.title: Check before changing the menu
sections.body: Investigate a pack size, ingredient price or observed portion before acting on an unexpected result. The kitchen confirms practice and the restaurant decides on changes.

pages.title: Restaurant bookkeeper, CPA or fractional CFO?
pages.heading: Match the adviser to the work you need.
pages.description: Compare the responsibilities of a bookkeeper, CPA and fractional CFO before deciding where your restaurant needs support.
pages.author: Ready Margin editorial
pages.keyword: restaurant bookkeeper vs CPA vs fractional CFO
pages.takeaway: Job titles are a starting point. Ask for the actual deliverables, cadence, approvals and boundaries in writing.

sections.title: Name the gap
sections.body: Identify whether the records are behind, the reports are unclear or a financial decision needs deeper review. Use one recent example to show where work stopped.

sections.title: Bookkeeping and recurring records
sections.body: Bookkeeping commonly covers transaction recording and reconciliation. Confirm whether restaurant settlements, close preparation, reporting and exception follow-up are included.

sections.title: CPA and specialist work
sections.body: A CPA may provide accounting, tax or assurance services under a defined engagement. Confirm who handles filings, advice and notices rather than relying on the job title.

sections.title: CFO-level review
sections.body: Financial guidance connects performance and cash with decisions about growth, operations or commitments. Its usefulness depends on the quality of the underlying records.

sections.title: Agree the connections
sections.body: Name who supplies inputs, resolves discrepancies and acts after a review. Ready Margin can combine recurring finance work and advisory support in a defined scope.

pages.title: Restaurant delivery-platform reconciliation
pages.heading: Reconcile the payout, not just the sales total.
pages.description: Connect delivery-platform sales, fees, refunds, settlement statements and bank receipts for the same period.
pages.author: Ready Margin editorial
pages.takeaway: Reconcile each settlement to its source period and adjustments before comparing it with a bank deposit.

sections.title: Identify the settlement
sections.body: Record the platform, statement period and expected payout date. Preserve the original statement so the deposit can be traced.

sections.title: Separate the components
sections.body: Review sales, fees, refunds and adjustments rather than treating the net deposit as gross revenue. Confirm account treatment with the person maintaining the books.

sections.title: Check timing
sections.body: Compare the payout reference and dates with bank activity. A deposit arriving later than the sales period requires a timing explanation.

sections.title: List the exceptions
sections.body: Record missing statements and unexplained deductions with their source amounts, responsible contact and next check date.

sections.title: Bring the answer into the close
sections.body: Keep settlement findings beside the cash and accounting review. System access and any direct platform connection are confirmed before service begins.

pages.title: Restaurant compliance records and handoffs
pages.heading: A compliance reminder needs a complete handoff.
pages.description: Organize confirmed requirements, source documents, internal cutoffs and evidence of completion for the responsible people.
pages.author: Ready Margin editorial
pages.keyword: restaurant compliance calendar and document handoff
pages.takeaway: A working calendar connects each confirmed obligation to its records, preparer, approver and completion evidence.

sections.title: Confirm what applies
sections.body: Start with requirements verified for the business, location and activity by the relevant authority or adviser. A generic checklist does not establish legal obligations or filing dates.

sections.title: Record the responsibility
sections.body: Name the preparer, approver and person completing the required action. Set an internal cutoff before the confirmed external deadline.

sections.title: Keep the approved documents
sections.body: Retain the version approved for the handoff and identify anything missing. Use the record-sharing arrangements agreed for the engagement.

sections.title: Keep completion evidence
sections.body: A checked reminder does not establish that an action was completed. Keep the relevant receipt or confirmation and the person who reviewed it.

sections.title: Confirm specialist involvement
sections.body: Name the filing, advice and escalation responsibilities in the scope. Outsourcing a supporting task does not remove the restaurant’s obligations.

pages.title: Restaurant payroll services: what the handoff should make clear
pages.heading: What a restaurant payroll service should check.
pages.description: Follow hours, tip inputs and corrections from the operating records through the payroll approval process.
pages.author: Ready Margin editorial
pages.keyword: restaurant payroll services, restaurant payroll support, payroll preparation for restaurants
pages.takeaway: A reliable payroll handoff names the period, the records, the approver and the route for exceptions before the deadline is close.

sections.title: Set the cycle first
sections.body: Agree the pay period, input deadline and approval cutoff before collecting corrections. Name the person coordinating outstanding questions.

sections.title: Compare the shift records
sections.body: Use schedules, recorded time and manager notes for the same shift. Keep the explanation attached to any change.

sections.title: Review tip inputs
sections.body: Check the source, period and documented restaurant policy. Confirm unusual amounts with authorized contacts before preparing the approval.

sections.title: Separate preparation and authorization
sections.body: The support team prepares the record; the nominated approver decides whether it is ready. Processing and tax responsibilities must be named in the engagement.

sections.title: Plan for late changes
sections.body: Agree how corrections are recorded, who decides after cutoff and which version reaches payroll. Employment and tax advice require the appropriate professional.

pages.title: Restaurant bookkeeping services: what reliable records need each week
pages.heading: What belongs in a restaurant bookkeeping routine.
pages.description: Keep sales settlements, bills, payroll records and account reconciliation moving toward the monthly close.
pages.author: Ready Margin editorial
pages.keyword: restaurant bookkeeping services, restaurant accounting support, outsourced restaurant bookkeeping
pages.takeaway: Reliable restaurant bookkeeping depends on timely source records, consistent treatment and an open-item list that does not disappear at month-end.

sections.title: Agree the inputs
sections.body: Bank activity, settlement statements, invoices and payroll records arrive on different dates. Define how each reaches the work file and who answers missing-record questions.

sections.title: Distinguish sales and receipts
sections.body: A sales report, settlement statement and bank deposit describe different steps. Connect the references and explain date or amount differences.

sections.title: Keep bill status clear
sections.body: Approved, disputed, incomplete and unpaid are separate states. Keep the supporting document and the person responsible for the next action together.

sections.title: Investigate unmatched activity
sections.body: Reconciliation should show what cleared, what remains pending and what needs explanation. Unresolved items need a dated review and contact.

sections.title: Confirm the recurring scope
sections.body: State whether the service includes close preparation, reports and exception follow-up. Tax work and historic cleanup may need separate arrangements.

pages.title: Restaurant cash flow management: turn a bank balance into a weekly plan
pages.seoTitle: Restaurant Cash Flow: A Weekly Review
pages.heading: Read cash with the commitments beside it.
pages.description: Review dated balances, expected receipts and obligations before the next restaurant cash decision.
pages.author: Ready Margin editorial
pages.keyword: restaurant cash flow management, restaurant cash flow support, weekly cash flow review for restaurants
pages.takeaway: A useful cash view is dated, explicit about known commitments and clear about what is estimated or still unconfirmed.

sections.title: Date the starting balance
sections.body: Identify the account and observation date. List expected receipts and commitments before the next review.

sections.title: Label estimates
sections.body: Distinguish approved amounts and source-backed receipts from timing assumptions or unanswered questions.

sections.title: Compare sales and settlement timing
sections.body: Strong trading may produce cash in another period. Check card and delivery settlements, refunds and fees against the operating records.

sections.title: Put obligations on the timeline
sections.body: Record payroll, bills, rent, taxes and other known commitments with their dates and approvers. Identify any question affecting the timing.

sections.title: Update before acting
sections.body: Confirm a receipt, resolve a bill or refresh the forecast before making the relevant decision. A projection states its assumptions and cannot guarantee future cash.

pages.title: Restaurant labor cost management: look beyond the schedule
pages.seoTitle: Restaurant Labor Cost: Hours, Pay & Sales
pages.heading: Review labor cost with comparable records.
pages.description: Connect sales, schedules, attendance and pay inputs before deciding what a labor-cost change means.
pages.author: Ready Margin editorial
pages.keyword: restaurant labor cost management, restaurant labor cost support, restaurant scheduling and payroll
pages.takeaway: A labor-cost review is more reliable when the sales period, schedule, recorded time and pay inputs describe the same operating week.

sections.title: Set a common period
sections.body: Use comparable dates for sales, planned hours and recorded time. Note a payroll period that covers a different set of trading days.

sections.title: Review plan and actual together
sections.body: The schedule shows planned coverage; time records show recorded hours. Manager context explains a cover shift, early close or unusual service.

sections.title: Resolve pay-input questions
sections.body: Missing punches, rate changes and tip corrections need a responsible contact. Keep the confirmed answer available to payroll and reporting.

sections.title: Use a relevant comparison
sections.body: Format, menu, hours and service model affect labor needs. Compare the restaurant’s plan and history using similar weeks.

sections.title: Choose the next check
sections.body: The response may be a record correction, shift-pattern review or clearer approval process. Staffing and pay decisions require management judgment and appropriate advice.

pages.description: Explore example workflows for payroll, supplier bills and cash. The scenarios use fictional records.

pages.title: A missing punch before payroll
pages.heading: A missing clock-out before payroll cutoff.
pages.description: A fictional workflow showing how a time-record question is checked and prepared for approval.

sections.title: Identify the missing input
sections.body: The shift has a recorded start but no confirmed finish time. Scheduled hours alone cannot establish what happened.

sections.title: Ask the manager
sections.body: Compare the schedule and attendance source, then obtain confirmation from the manager who knows the shift.

sections.title: Keep the correction traceable
sections.body: Record the reason, changed input and confirmation. Flag anything still unresolved at cutoff.

sections.title: Present the approval
sections.body: The restaurant’s approver receives the prepared record and remaining questions. This is an example process, not a customer outcome.

pages.title: A supplier price change worth checking
pages.heading: The regular delivery with a different total.
pages.description: A fictional supplier review that checks quantity, pack size and price before choosing the next action.

sections.title: Compare the delivery
sections.body: Check whether the same items and quantities were supplied. Identify substitutions and pack-size changes.

sections.title: Review the price basis
sections.body: Compare the available invoice, agreed pricing and credit records. Ask the supplier contact about any unexplained difference.

sections.title: Document the finding
sections.body: Keep the confirmed explanation with the purchasing records. It can inform an invoice query or recipe-cost update.

sections.title: Decide on the response
sections.body: The restaurant authorizes payments and operating changes. This example illustrates the review; it does not represent achieved savings.

pages.keyword: A supplier price change worth checking

pages.title: Sales are strong. Cash still needs a plan.
pages.heading: Strong sales before a busy payment week.
pages.description: A fictional cash review connecting settlement timing and known obligations to the next financial decision.

sections.title: Date the balance
sections.body: Identify the accounts and observation date. Compare sales with settled receipts.

sections.title: List the commitments
sections.body: Place payroll, supplier bills and other known amounts on the payment timeline. Label estimates and missing inputs.

sections.title: Confirm the timing
sections.body: Investigate a receipt still pending or an obligation without a confirmed date.

sections.title: Review the decision
sections.body: Bring the findings to the owner before payment priorities are set. This example does not guarantee cash availability.

pages.keyword: Sales are strong. Cash still needs a plan.

pages.title: Why restaurant sales do not equal available cash
pages.heading: A sales week and a cash week can differ.
pages.description: Compare trading activity with receipts, settlement timing and upcoming obligations before reading the available cash.

sections.title: Separate the records
sections.body: Sales describe what was sold. The bank shows settled receipts. Existing commitments affect how much of that cash is available.

sections.title: Confirm the arrival date
sections.body: Check settlements, refunds and fees against bank activity. Establish timing differences from source records.

sections.title: Add the obligations
sections.body: Place known payroll and supplier commitments beside the dated balance. Mark estimates and incomplete information.

sections.title: Assign the unanswered question
sections.body: Name who will confirm a missing receipt or bill and when. Refresh the view before the payment decision.

pages.takeaway: Read the balance with settlement dates and known commitments—not on its own.
pages.author: Ready Margin editorial
pages.keyword: Why restaurant sales do not equal available cash

pages.title: A calmer payroll handoff starts before cutoff
pages.heading: Four checks before payroll cutoff.
pages.description: Confirm the pay period, exceptions, approver and final version before the restaurant’s payroll handoff.

sections.title: Confirm the period
sections.body: Schedules, attendance and tip inputs must cover the dates being prepared for payroll.

sections.title: Collect the exceptions
sections.body: List missing punches, changed shifts and incomplete tip records with the manager confirming each item.

sections.title: Name the approver
sections.body: State who authorizes payroll and when the prepared records must arrive.

sections.title: Check the final version
sections.body: Confirm that approved corrections reached the payroll input. Keep a route for changes received after cutoff.

pages.takeaway: Check that each correction reached the final record before it goes for approval.
pages.author: Ready Margin editorial
pages.keyword: A calmer payroll handoff starts before cutoff

pages.title: Food cost moved. Which question comes first?
pages.heading: Check the cause behind a food-cost change.
pages.description: Review periods, prices, quantities and kitchen records before deciding what to change.

sections.title: Check the comparison
sections.body: Use the same period, item and unit. Confirm any pack-size or delivery-date difference.

sections.title: Review the kitchen inputs
sections.body: Use current recipes, yields, portions, counts and available waste records. Identify estimates.

sections.title: Investigate the strongest lead
sections.body: Ask the purchasing or kitchen contact to confirm the record most likely to explain the movement.

sections.title: Bring the finding to the decision
sections.body: Document what was confirmed before discussing an order, recipe or operating change. A percentage alone does not establish the response.

pages.takeaway: Check the records behind the change before deciding what to change in the restaurant.
pages.author: Ready Margin editorial
pages.keyword: Food cost moved. Which question comes first?

pages.title: The attendance questions to settle before payroll
pages.heading: Confirm the shift before changing the time record.
pages.description: Connect the schedule, recorded hours and manager confirmation before payroll preparation.

sections.title: Compare the sources
sections.body: Review schedule, attendance and notes for the same shift. A difference may reflect an approved operating change.

sections.title: Confirm with the manager
sections.body: Ask the person who knows the shift to verify what happened. Keep the confirmation with the correction.

sections.title: Set a decision deadline
sections.body: If the answer is missing near cutoff, tell the approver which input is unresolved and who is checking it.

sections.title: Address repeated exceptions
sections.body: Repeated corrections may point to the shift-change or timekeeping process. Review that process at the next cycle.

pages.takeaway: Keep the manager’s confirmation connected to the corrected attendance record.
pages.author: Ready Margin editorial
pages.keyword: The attendance questions to settle before payroll

pages.title: A useful supplier bill review goes beyond the total
pages.heading: Review the bill against the delivery.
pages.description: Check quantities, pack sizes, prices and credits before presenting a supplier invoice for approval.

sections.title: Collect the documents
sections.body: Use the order, delivery record and invoice where available. Identify missing evidence.

sections.title: Compare the units
sections.body: Check quantity and pack size before comparing price. Review substitutions, credits and changes to the order.

sections.title: Get the relevant answer
sections.body: The receiving manager confirms deliveries; the supplier contact resolves pricing questions. Payment approval remains with the nominated person.

sections.title: Keep the explanation
sections.body: Save the confirmed answer with the vendor record so repeated questions can be checked against it.

pages.takeaway: Compare the order, delivery and invoice before treating a total as a price change.
pages.author: Ready Margin editorial
pages.keyword: A useful supplier bill review goes beyond the total

pages.title: Five questions for a useful weekly P&L review
pages.heading: Five checks for your weekly P&L.
pages.description: Confirm dates, missing inputs, material movements and operating context before choosing the next action.

sections.title: 1. Check the dates
sections.body: Confirm the period and comparison dates. Different trading-day counts or cutoffs can distort the movement.

sections.title: 2. Check what is missing
sections.body: Identify incomplete bills, payroll inputs or other records. Label provisional figures.

sections.title: 3. Find the material change
sections.body: Use supporting records to separate timing, volume and cost movement.

sections.title: 4. Ask about the operation
sections.body: Changes in trading, staffing, purchasing and service belong beside the financial explanation.

sections.title: 5. Choose the next action
sections.body: Name the decision or check, the person responsible and its review date. Confirm missing evidence before drawing a conclusion.

pages.takeaway: A useful P&L review connects the period, completeness and operating context to a decision.
pages.author: Ready Margin editorial
pages.keyword: Five questions for a useful weekly P&L review

pages.title: Compare locations without losing their context
pages.heading: Compare locations on a consistent basis.
pages.description: Align periods and account definitions while keeping each restaurant’s operating conditions visible.

sections.title: Define the reporting basis
sections.body: Use consistent dates and account treatment across the group. Document differences in allocation or entity coverage.

sections.title: Retain local context
sections.body: Different formats, opening hours and recent changes can explain results. Include that context in the comparison.

sections.title: Identify incomplete inputs
sections.body: A late bill or payroll input at one location can distort the group picture. State when it will be updated.

sections.title: Discuss the exception locally
sections.body: Use the finding to ask the manager a specific question. Shared reports should help explain performance rather than erase differences.

pages.takeaway: Standardize the reporting basis, then explain the differences that still matter.
pages.author: Ready Margin editorial
pages.keyword: Compare locations without losing their context

sections.title: Name what cannot wait

sections.body: Bring recent records and known obligations through the agreed sharing route. Label incomplete or estimated information.

sections.title: Set a workable sequence

sections.title: Update the plan

pages.takeaway: Start with the decision and deadline, then gather the records needed to address it.

pages.title: Website privacy notice
pages.heading: How we handle website information.
pages.description: Information used to respond to enquiries, store preferences and measure the website when you allow it.

sections.title: Your enquiry
sections.body: The form collects contact details and optional restaurant context so we can respond and arrange a conversation. Do not submit passwords, bank details or employee payroll records.

sections.title: Enquiry delivery
sections.body: An approved delivery provider is used when online enquiries are enabled. A failed request offers an email route. Provider names and retention periods require business approval.

sections.title: Optional measurement
sections.body: Analytics are off by default. On the Vercel-hosted website, Allow enables Vercel Web Analytics and Speed Insights. Reported URLs exclude query strings and fragments; form values and diagnostic answers are excluded. Change your choice in the footer.

sections.title: Contact and pending details
sections.body: Email contact@readymargin.com about your enquiry or this notice. The legal entity, business address, rights process and retention periods require approval before the production business launch.

pages.title: Website terms

pages.description: Website information and examples sit alongside the separate agreement defining any service we provide.

sections.title: Service agreements
sections.body: The website describes managed services and provides general operating information. A separate agreement confirms the work, responsibilities, timing and fees.

sections.title: Examples and availability
sections.body: Example workflows do not represent customer results. Future technology is not presented as generally available. No profit, savings or particular outcome is guaranteed.

sections.title: Website materials
sections.body: Ready Margin text, artwork and other materials carry their applicable rights and licences. Ask before reproducing branded materials.

sections.title: Details pending review
sections.body: The contracting entity, governing law, dispute provisions and complete contractual terms require legal review before the production business launch. Questions can be sent to contact@readymargin.com.

pages.title: Cookie & analytics choices
pages.heading: Your website preferences.
pages.description: Choose whether to allow optional measurement and reopen that choice from the footer.

sections.title: Local preferences
sections.body: The browser can store your analytics choice and display preferences. They support this experience and are not used to identify you across websites.

sections.title: Optional analytics
sections.body: Optional measurement stays off until you choose Allow. Permitted interactions are recorded only when a measurement service is connected. You can reject it or change your choice.

sections.title: Change your choice
sections.body: Cookie choices in the footer reopens the controls. Withdrawal stops future optional events; it does not erase events already received by a configured provider.

sections.title: Provider review
sections.body: The production provider and cookie inventory must be reviewed whenever integrations change.

pages.title: Accessibility
pages.heading: Browsing Ready Margin accessibly.
pages.description: Our approach to navigation, motion and reporting a barrier.

sections.title: Navigation and controls
sections.body: The website uses semantic headings, labelled controls, visible focus, a skip link and keyboard-operable navigation. Motion has reduced-motion and static alternatives.

sections.title: Display and movement
sections.body: Your device’s reduced-motion setting disables content movement. Text can be enlarged and layouts adapt to narrow screens.

sections.title: Report a barrier
sections.body: Email contact@readymargin.com with the page and the difficulty you encountered. You may include your browser or assistive technology if you wish.

sections.title: Continued review
sections.body: We work to resolve barriers as the website changes. This statement does not claim independent certification or universal compatibility.

faqs.question: What can Ready Margin handle?
faqs.answer: Bookkeeping, accounting, payroll preparation, tip inputs, bills, cost review and financial guidance. We’ll agree the exact work and responsibilities in your proposal.

faqs.question: Is Ready Margin a service or software?
faqs.answer: A managed finance service supported by a workspace. Our team handles the work in your scope and reviews the findings with you. The public workspace shows the process using sample records.

faqs.question: Can we keep our current systems?
faqs.answer: We start with the tools you already use. Access, exports and compatibility are reviewed before the service begins. Any direct connections are confirmed during onboarding.

faqs.question: Is the first demo free?
faqs.answer: Yes. We’ll show you how the service works, discuss your priorities and answer your questions. There is no commitment to a package.

faqs.question: How is my price worked out?
faqs.answer: Your locations, systems, payroll complexity and chosen support determine the work involved. After your demo, we can prepare a tailored quote with the scope and fees in writing.

faqs.question: What should I bring to the demo?
faqs.answer: The names of your systems and one example of work you need help with. A few notes are enough; detailed financial or employee records can follow through an agreed sharing process.
